title: The wild man by the river (Mark 1:4–8)
hookLine: John the Baptist in camel hair calls people to turn around

lines: CAMEL HAIR AND A LEATHER BELT.
CROWDS WALK OUT TO HEAR HIM.
cards: A man lives out in the wild. Rough clothes woven from camel hair, a leather belt. He eats what he can find: locusts and wild honey.
No house, no title, no invitation. And crowds walk out of the city to hear him. Mark's Gospel doesn't open with a manger.

It opens here, in the desert by the Jordan River, with this man shouting. His name is John, and people will call him John the Baptist. The whole region of Judea went out to him, Mark says, and people from Jerusalem too.
What was he saying that was worth the walk?

teach.h: A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.
teach.b: Mark begins with the prophet Isaiah, in the King James Bible: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight."
Then: "John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins." Repentance is a heavy church word.
The Greek is metanoia, built on the word for mind: a change of mind.
The Hebrew prophets used a simpler word, shuv: turn around, go back. So the picture isn't mainly groveling. It's a person walking the wrong way who stops, turns, and heads home.
Then John washes them in the river. Water had long been used in Jewish life for washing and becoming clean, and John makes it a sign of a fresh start.
His clothes are a message too: the Bible describes the prophet Elijah the same way, hairy, with a leather belt.

teach.h: NOT WORTHY TO UNTIE HIS SANDALS.
teach.b: Then the surprise, in what John says about himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Untying sandals was a servant's job.
John has crowds, fame, a following, and he spends it all pointing past himself.

teach.h: PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.
teach.b: I baptize you with water, he says; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. His whole job is to get people turned around and facing the right way, so they'll recognize the one who's coming.
The Jewish historian Josephus remembered him too, as a good man who called people to live justly.

how: Many Christians remember John the Baptist during Advent, the weeks before Christmas, when his call to prepare the way is read in church. His birth is celebrated on June 24, and in many traditions repentance is practiced through confession, private or shared, and a fresh start.

o: a deep feeling of shame for sin
a change of mind, a turning around
a promise to give money to the poor

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: repentance in the Greek is mainly about feeling bad
metanoia means a change of mind, a turning around.
John's clothes echo the prophet Elijah
the Bible describes Elijah as hairy, with a leather belt.
John called himself the greatest of the prophets
he said he wasn't worthy to untie the sandals of the one coming after him.

games.q: you're John. crowds from all Judea and Jerusalem are coming out to hear you. they'd follow you anywhere. what do you tell them?
o: that you are the one they've been waiting for.
that one mightier is coming, and you're not worthy to untie his sandals.
to go back home and forget about it.
games.why: at the height of his fame, John points past himself: there cometh one mightier than I after me.

practice: Think about direction, not guilt: is there one small thing you keep walking toward that takes you somewhere you don't want to go, a habit, a tone of voice with someone, a scroll at midnight, a grudge?
Name it quietly, then picture yourself stopping and turning around, not a big dramatic scene, just a turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning.

wordCard.voice: Metanoia. The Greek word for repentance, built on the word for mind: a change of mind, a turning around, the thing John called the crowds to do.

orig.note: Greek: repentance. Built on the word for mind: a change of mind, a turning around.

carryVoice: Your line: turn around. start again. Until tomorrow, when someone new walks down to John's river.
